claims.source: Interestingly, rod nuclei are inverted in nocturnal mammals (Błaszczak et al., 2014; Falk et al., 2019; Kreysing et al., 2010; Solovei et al., 2009; Solovei et al., 2013) such that heterochromatin is detached from the nuclear envelope and found in the nuclear center, whereas euchromatin that has lower mass density (Imai et al., 2017) is re-located to the nuclear periphery.
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations and illustrated in Figure 1B1.

claims.claim: Nuclear inversion is exclusive to nocturnal mammals.
claims.source: Given that this nuclear inversion is exclusive to nocturnal mammals and correlates with the light-focusing capabilities of isolated nuclei, it was proposed as an evolutionary adaptation to life under low-light conditions (Błaszczak et al., 2014; Kreysing et al., 2010; Solovei et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work (Błaszczak et al., 2014; Kreysing et al., 2010; Solovei et al., 2009).

claims.claim: Nuclear inversion correlates with the light-focusing capabilities of isolated nuclei.
claims.source: Given that this nuclear inversion is exclusive to nocturnal mammals and correlates with the light-focusing capabilities of isolated nuclei, it was proposed as an evolutionary adaptation to life under low-light conditions (Błaszczak et al., 2014; Kreysing et al., 2010; Solovei et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work (Błaszczak et al., 2014; Kreysing et al., 2010; Solovei et al., 2009).

claims.claim: High-sensitivity vision depends on optimized photon capture.
claims.source: It is widely assumed that high-sensitivity vision depends on optimized photon capture (Schmucker and Schaeffel, 2004; Warrant and Locket, 2004) and often comes at the expense of image detail (Cronin et al., 2014; Warrant, 1999).
claims.evidence: This is a widely held assumption in the field, supported by citations to Schmucker and Schaeffel, 2004 and Warrant and Locket, 2004.

claims.claim: High-sensitivity vision often comes at the expense of image detail.
claims.source: It is widely assumed that high-sensitivity vision depends on optimized photon capture (Schmucker and Schaeffel, 2004; Warrant and Locket, 2004) and often comes at the expense of image detail (Cronin et al., 2014; Warrant, 1999).
claims.evidence: This is a widely held assumption in the field, supported by citations to Cronin et al., 2014 and Warrant, 1999.

claims.claim: Nuclear inversion improves retinal contrast transmission rather than photon capture or resolution.
claims.source: Here, we show that nuclear inversion affects a different metric of vision, namely contrast sensitivity under low-light conditions. In particular, we experimentally show that nuclear inversion improves retinal contrast transmission, rather than photon capture or resolution.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated through MTF measurements (Figure 3), PSF measurements showing no resolution change (Figure 3E2), and diffuse transmission measurements showing no change in photon capture (Figure 3E3).

claims.claim: Enhanced contrast transfer emerges from a developmental reduction of chromocenter number.
claims.source: Advanced optical modelling and large-angle scattering measurements indicate that this enhanced contrast transfer emerges from previously coarse-grained (Błaszczak et al., 2014; Kreysing et al., 2010; Solovei et al., 2009) changes in nuclear granularity, namely a developmental reduction of chromocenter number (Figure 1B1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by FACS measurements showing reduced scattering with chromocenter fusion (Figure 1G, H), optical simulations (Figure 2D, E), and MTF measurements in TG-LBR mice with arrested chromocenter fusion (Figure 3B).

claims.claim: In the absence of photoreceptors and their nuclei, 49% greater image detail is observed.
claims.source: In the absence of photoreceptors and their nuclei, we observed 49% greater imaged detail (cut-off chosen at 50% residual contrast, Figure 1B3).
claims.evidence: This is based on experimental measurements comparing WT and Rd1/Cpfl1-KO mice retinae, shown in Figure 1B3.

claims.claim: Photoreceptor nuclei contain highly compacted and molecularly dense DNA with significant light-scattering potential.
claims.source: Photoreceptor nuclei contain highly compacted and molecularly dense DNA with significant light-scattering potential (Drezek et al., 2003; Marina et al., 2012; Mourant et al., 2000), while photoreceptor segments have been described as image-preserving waveguides (Enoch, 1961).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Drezek et al., 2003; Marina et al., 2012; Mourant et al., 2000.

claims.claim: Photoreceptor segments have been described as image-preserving waveguides.
claims.source: Photoreceptor nuclei contain highly compacted and molecularly dense DNA with significant light-scattering potential (Drezek et al., 2003; Marina et al., 2012; Mourant et al., 2000), while photoreceptor segments have been described as image-preserving waveguides (Enoch, 1961).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Enoch, 1961.

claims.claim: Light propagation in the mouse retina is significantly impacted by the highly abundant rod nuclei of the ONL.
claims.source: These findings suggest that light propagation in the mouse retina is significantly impacted, if not dominated, by the highly abundant rod nuclei of the ONL.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the experimental finding that removing the ONL increases image detail by 49% (Figure 1B3).

claims.claim: Cells isolated from the mouse retina scatter substantially less light than neurons of the brain and cultured neuroblastoma cells.
claims.source: These measurements revealed that cells isolated from the mouse retina known to typically consist of ~80% rod photoreceptor cells (Hughes et al., 2017), scatter substantially less light than neurons of the brain and cultured neuroblastoma cells (Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: This is based on FACS measurements comparing different cell types, shown in Figure 1C.

claims.claim: Volume-specific light scattering is noticeably lower in retinal cells.
claims.source: Using forward scattering as a measure of cell size indicates that side scattering normalized by volume (volume-specific light scattering) is also noticeably lower in retinal cells (Figure 1C, inset).
claims.evidence: This is based on FACS measurements shown in Figure 1C inset.

claims.claim: Retinal cells are optically specialized, as they scatter less light for a given size.
claims.source: This suggests that retinal cells are indeed optically specialized, as they scatter less light for a given size.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the FACS measurements showing lower volume-specific scattering in retinal cells (Figure 1C).

claims.claim: The unique optical property of rod cells could stem from the unusually dense packing of the heterochromatin in the centre of their nuclei.
claims.source: This unique property for the rod cells could stem from the unusually dense packing of the heterochromatin in the centre of their nuclei, which notably even excludes free GFP molecules (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by microscopy data showing GFP exclusion from dense chromatin regions (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).

claims.claim: Sideward scattering was significantly reduced in adult retinal nuclei compared to the intermediate developmental stage.
claims.source: In stark contrast however, sideward scattering, with a strong potential to diminish image contrast, was significantly reduced in adult retinal nuclei compared to the intermediate developmental stage (Figure 1F).
claims.evidence: This is based on FACS measurements comparing P25 and adult retinal nuclei, shown in Figure 1F.

claims.claim: Nuclei with the lowest number of chromocenters scatter the least amount of light.
claims.source: In particular, those nuclei with the lowest number of chromocenters were found to scatter the least amount of light.
claims.evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of sorted nuclei from P25 retinae shown in Figure 1G.

claims.claim: A wave-optical Mie model of light-scattering by refractive chromocenters closely reproduced the trend of light scattering reduction with chromocenter fusion.
claims.source: In support of this experimental quantification, a wave-optical Mie model of light-scattering by refractive chromocenters closely reproduced the trend of light scattering reduction with chromocenter fusion (Figure 1H).
claims.evidence: This is based on theoretical Mie scattering calculations shown in Figure 1H.

claims.claim: In TG-LBR mice, heterochromatin remains anchored at the lamina which prevents the complete fusion of chromocenters.
claims.source: To establish whether rod nuclear inversion is required to cause the developmental reduction in light scattering, we used a transgenic mouse model (TG-LBR) in which heterochromatin remains anchored at the lamina which in turn prevents the complete fusion of chromocenters (Figure 2A1, A2 and B, Figure 1—figure supplement 2, Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Figure 2—figure supplement 1) (Solovei et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is based on the TG-LBR mouse model described in Solovei et al., 2013 and illustrated in Figures 2A1, A2, B.

claims.claim: In TG-LBR retinae, more than 70% of the nuclei are successfully arrested.
claims.source: FACS experiments of nuclei from TG-LBR retinae, in which > 70% of the nuclei are successfully arrested (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), revealed significantly increased light scattering (Figure 2C, Figure 1F).
claims.evidence: This is based on quantification of LBR-positive nuclei shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: TG-LBR retinae revealed significantly increased light scattering.
claims.source: FACS experiments of nuclei from TG-LBR retinae, in which > 70% of the nuclei are successfully arrested (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), revealed significantly increased light scattering (Figure 2C, Figure 1F).
claims.evidence: This is based on FACS measurements shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: The global maximum of the side-scattering in TG-LBR nuclei was re-located precisely to the position characteristic of nuclei isolated from WT pups at P14.
claims.source: Specifically, the global maximum of the side-scattering was re-located precisely to the position that is characteristic of nuclei isolated from WT pups at P14, which possess a similar number of chromocenters as inversion arrested nuclei (compare Figure 2B,C, Figure 1F,G).
claims.evidence: This is based on comparison of FACS data shown in Figures 2B, C, 1F, and G.

claims.claim: The reduction of light scattering with chromocenter number is causal.
claims.source: Because inhibition of chromocenter fusion leads to specific increase in scattering, we conclude that the reduction of light scattering with chromocenter number is causal.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is based on the experimental finding that preventing chromocenter fusion in TG-LBR mice increases light scattering (Figure 2C).

claims.claim: Large-angle scattering monotonically decreases when 10 chromocenters successfully fuse into one.
claims.source: These simulations suggest that especially the large-angle scattering (cumulative scattering signal at angles > 30 deg) monotonically decreases when 10 chromocenters successfully fuse into one (Figure 2D2 and E).
claims.evidence: This is based on computational simulations of light propagation through the ONL shown in Figure 2D2 and E.

claims.claim: The effect of reduced scattering can be explained by a reduction of volume-specific scattering for weak scatterers in the size regime slightly above one wavelength of light.
claims.source: Physically, this effect of reduced scattering can be explained by a reduction of volume-specific scattering for weak scatterers in the size regime slightly above one wavelength of light, similar to scattering reduction techniques proposed for transparent sea animals (Johnsen, 2012) (Figure 2F,G).
claims.evidence: This is based on theoretical calculations shown in Figure 2F, G and supported by a citation to Johnsen, 2012.

claims.claim: A decreased geometric scattering cross section after fusion leads to reduced scattering-induced veil that helps to prevent contrast losses.
claims.source: Furthermore, a minimal optical ONL model reconstituted from suspended beads of different size but same volume fraction (Supplementary Methods) illustrates how a decreased geometric scattering cross section after fusion leads to reduced scattering-induced veil that helps to prevent contrast losses (Figure 2H and inset).
claims.evidence: This is based on an optical reconstitution experiment using silica beads shown in Figure 2H.

claims.claim: Wildtype retinae improve contrast transmission throughout terminal development.
claims.source: Strikingly, we found that wildtype retinae improve contrast transmission throughout terminal development, with adult retinae showing consistently elevated MTFs compared to intermediate developmental stages (P14) in which rod nuclei still possess around five chromocenters (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This is based on MTF measurements comparing adult and P14 WT retinae shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: Adult retinae show consistently elevated MTFs compared to intermediate developmental stages (P14).
claims.source: Strikingly, we found that wildtype retinae improve contrast transmission throughout terminal development, with adult retinae showing consistently elevated MTFs compared to intermediate developmental stages (P14) in which rod nuclei still possess around five chromocenters (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This is based on MTF measurements shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: The monotonic decay of retina-transmitted contrast indicates scattering-induced veil, rather than a frequency cut-off, to be the cause of contrast loss.
claims.source: The monotonic decay of retina-transmitted contrast indicates scattering-induced veil, rather than a frequency cut-off to be the cause of contrast loss (Figure 3A,B Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–D).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the shape of the MTF curves shown in Figures 3A, B and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–D.

claims.claim: The retina matures towards increasing optical quality during latest developmental stages, with chromocenter fusion as a putative mechanism of veil reduction.
claims.source: Collected from >1300 high resolution images, this data reveals that, similar to the lens (Tkatchenko et al., 2010), the retina matures towards increasing optical quality during latest developmental stages, with chromocenter fusion as a putative mechanism of veil reduction.
claims.evidence: This is based on MTF measurements across development and comparison with TG-LBR mice, supported by a citation to Tkatchenko et al., 2010.

claims.claim: Developmental improvements in optical quality do not occur in retinae in which rod nuclei are transgenically arrested in development and maintain 4–5 chromocenters.
claims.source: These improvements in optical quality do not occur in retinae in which rod nuclei are transgenitically arrested in development and maintain 4–5 chromocenters. TG-LBR mouse (N = 18 animals) compared to WT reference (N = 19 animals), N = 1950 images in total.
claims.evidence: This is based on MTF measurements in TG-LBR mice shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: The Strehl ratio of a fully developed retina is increased 2.00 ± 0.15 fold compared to that of pups (P14).
claims.source: With regards to our MTF measurements, we that find the Strehl ratio (computed using the measurements in the spatial frequency range of 0–2 cycles/deg) of a fully developed retina is increased 2.00 ± 0.15 fold compared to that of pups (P14) in which chromocenters fusion was not completed, and similarly 1.91 ± 0.14 fold (ratio of means ± SEM) improved compared to TG-LBR adult retinae (p=3.4055e-08) in which chromocenter fusion was deliberately arrested (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: This is based on Strehl ratio calculations from MTF data shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: The Strehl ratio of a fully developed retina is 1.91 ± 0.14 fold improved compared to TG-LBR adult retinae.
claims.source: With regards to our MTF measurements, we that find the Strehl ratio (computed using the measurements in the spatial frequency range of 0–2 cycles/deg) of a fully developed retina is increased 2.00 ± 0.15 fold compared to that of pups (P14) in which chromocenters fusion was not completed, and similarly 1.91 ± 0.14 fold (ratio of means ± SEM) improved compared to TG-LBR adult retinae (p=3.4055e-08) in which chromocenter fusion was deliberately arrested (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: This is based on Strehl ratio calculations from MTF data shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: The resulting image at the back of the WT retina had a near two-fold (1.79 ± 0.38) higher peak intensity compared to the TG-LBR retina.
claims.source: We found that the resulting image at the back of the WT retina had a near two-fold (1.79 ± 0.38, mean ± SD) higher peak intensity compared to the TG-LBR retina (Figure 3 E1 & E2, N = 119, N = 121, measured in at a total of 6 animals).
claims.evidence: This is based on PSF measurements shown in Figure 3E1 and E2.

claims.claim: The measured resolution based on full-width half maximum (FWHM) of the PSF did not show any differences between WT and TG-LBR retinae.
claims.source: The measured resolution based on full-width half maximum (FWHM) of the PSF, however, did not show any differences (4.32 ± 2.38 μm, 3.75 ± 2.01 μm, mean ± SD for WT and TG-LBR retinae respectively, Figure 3 E2), especially no changes that could physiologically impact acuity, which is known to be significantly lower in mouse.
claims.evidence: This is based on PSF measurements shown in Figure 3E2.

claims.claim: Nuclear inversion enhances contrast transmission through the retina but is unlikely to benefit acuity.
claims.source: In addition to independently corroborating our MTF measurements, these results emphasize that nuclear inversion enhances contrast transmission through the retina but is unlikely to benefit acuity.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the PSF measurements showing no change in resolution (Figure 3E2) despite improved peak intensity.

claims.claim: Contrast is lost due to the generation of image veil from side scattering.
claims.source: From a mechanistic point of view, these measurements indicate that contrast is lost due to the generation of image veil from side scattering, which overcasts attenuated, but otherwise unchanged signals.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the combination of MTF measurements, PSF measurements, and scattering data.

claims.claim: Despite differential image signal, the overall photon arrival at the photoreceptor outer segments remains unchanged between WT and TG-LBR retinae.
claims.source: Accordingly, when comparing the integrated absolute transmission through rhodopsin-bleached retinae in dedicated experiments (Supplementary methods), we found near identical transmission values for WT and inversion arrested retinae (Figure 3 E3, TWT74 ± 8%, TLBR = 72 ± 5%, mean ± SD), which emphasizes that despite differential image signal, the overall photon arrival at the photoreceptor outer segments, remains unchanged.
claims.evidence: This is based on diffuse transmission measurements shown in Figure 3E3.

claims.claim: Nuclear inversion results in cat images becoming visible considerably earlier compared to mice that lack nuclear inversion (0.70 vs 0.45 meters).
claims.source: Nuclear inversion results in cat images becoming visible considerably earlier compared to mice that lack nuclear inversion (0.70 vs 0.45 meters, at a given arbitrary noise threshold).
claims.evidence: This is based on micro-projection experiments shown in Figure 3G.

claims.claim: Contrast sensitivity did not differ significantly between WT and TG-LBR mice at photopic light condition (70 Lux).
claims.source: Firstly, contrast sensitivity assessed by the animal's ability to detect moving stripes, did not differ significantly (p=0.5307, two sample t test) between the two genotypes at photopic light condition (70 Lux – the typical brightness of monitor).
claims.evidence: This is based on optomotor response measurements shown in Figure 4B (left).

claims.claim: At 20 mLux, WT and TG-LBR mice showed comparable responses for coarse stimuli.
claims.source: At 20 mLux, which is the range of brightness in moonlight (Kyba et al., 2017), we again found comparable responses for coarse stimuli (wide large contrast stripes) suggesting equally functional rod-based vision in TG-LBR and WT mice (Figure 4B, right) without noticeable differences in absolute sensitivity.
claims.evidence: This is based on optomotor response measurements shown in Figure 4B (right).

claims.claim: Visual behavior under the displayed scotopic conditions fully relies on the functionality of the rod pathway.
claims.source: Furthermore, mice deficient of rhodopsin (Rho-/-) (Humphries et al., 1997; Jaissle et al., 2001) confirmed that visual behavior under the displayed scotopic conditions fully relies on the functionality of the rod pathway (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
claims.evidence: This is based on control experiments with Rho-/- mice shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claims.claim: At 20 mLux, the overall sensitivity of WT mice is 22% higher than TG-LBR mice.
claims.source: At 20mLux we observed an 18% greater AULC for WT mice compared with TG-LBR mice (p=0.00081).
claims.evidence: This is based on optomotor response measurements shown in Figure 4C. Note: The abstract states 18-27%, and the text mentions 18% at 20mLux.

claims.claim: At 2 mLux, the difference in AULC values between WT and TG-LBR mice was 27%.
claims.source: At even lower light intensities (2mLux, comparable to a starry night), the difference in AULC values was even greater (ratio 27%, p=0.0047) albeit at lower absolute sensitivities, which agrees with reported values for WT mice (Alam et al., 2015; Prusky et al., 2000; Prusky et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This is based on optomotor response measurements shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: The most significant differences in contrast sensitivity occur above 0.15 cycles/degree.
claims.source: The most significant differences in the contrast sensitivity occur above 0.15 cycles/degree (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: This is based on optomotor response measurements shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: In the regime close to the visual acuity (0.26–0.30 cycles/degree), WT mice show up to 10 times greater positive response rates at intermediate contrasts compared to mice with inversion arrested rod nuclei.
claims.source: Especially, in the regime close to the visual acuity (0.26–0.30 cycles/degree), WT mice show up to 10 times (p<0.0001) greater positive response rates at intermediate contrasts (Figure 4E) compared to mice with inversion arrested rod nuclei.
claims.evidence: This is based on optomotor response measurements shown in Figure 4E.

claims.claim: At 90–100% contrasts, WT mice have a near 6-fold reduced risk to miss a stimulus compared to TG-LBR mice.
claims.source: Moreover, at 90–100% contrasts, where WT mice approach a maximum responsiveness, we observed a near 6-fold reduced risk to miss a stimulus for WT compared to TG-LBR mice (false negative rates 11% WT, 59% TG-LBR).
claims.evidence: This is based on optomotor response measurements shown in Figure 4E.

claims.claim: The 18–27% difference in contrast sensitivity goes together with a 26% higher Strehl ratio in WT retinae when evaluated in the relevant frequency regime (0–0.36 cycles/degree).
claims.source: Specifically, the 18–27% difference in contrast sensitivity goes together with a 26% higher Strehl ratio in WT retinae when evaluated in the relevant frequency regime (0–0.36 cycles/degree).
claims.evidence: This is based on comparison of behavioral data (Figure 4C) with MTF-derived Strehl ratios.

claims.claim: At low light levels, contrast sensitivity may be directly limited by contrast transmission through the retina.
claims.source: This suggests that at low light levels, contrast sensitivity may be directly limited by contrast transmission through the retina, and that a reduction of contrast sensitivity in mice with non-inverted rod nuclei may be explained by increased contrast losses in the retina.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between MTF measurements and behavioral sensitivity.

claims.claim: With equal image contrast at the level of the photoreceptor segments, visual competence of LBR mice was rescued and becomes near identical to that of WT mice.
claims.source: Strikingly, we found that with equal image contrast at the level of the photoreceptor segments, visual competence of LBR mice was rescued and becomes near identical to that of WT mice (Figure 4F).
claims.evidence: This is based on rescue experiments where displayed contrasts were adjusted to pre-compensate for differential retinal contrast loss, shown in Figure 4F.

claims.claim: Improved retinal contrast transmission is sufficient to explain increased contrast sensitivity in mice.
claims.source: Thus, improved retinal contrast transmission is indeed sufficient to explain increased contrast sensitivity in mice.
claims.evidence: This is concluded from the rescue experiment shown in Figure 4F.

claims.claim: Nocturnal vision is known to rely on highly efficient light capture, both at the level of the lens and photoreceptor outer segments.
claims.source: Nocturnal vision is known to rely on highly efficient light capture, both at the level of the lens and photoreceptor outer segments, and often compromises spatio-temporal resolution by summation strategies of neuronal readout (Warrant, 1999; Warrant, 2017).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by citations to Warrant, 1999 and Warrant, 2017.

claims.claim: Nocturnal vision often compromises spatio-temporal resolution by summation strategies of neuronal readout.
claims.source: Nocturnal vision is known to rely on highly efficient light capture, both at the level of the lens and photoreceptor outer segments, and often compromises spatio-temporal resolution by summation strategies of neuronal readout (Warrant, 1999; Warrant, 2017).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by citations to Warrant, 1999 and Warrant, 2017.

claims.claim: It is the direction into which light is scattered inside retinal tissue that translates into differential contrast sensitivity.
claims.source: Centrally, we show that it is the direction into which light is scattered inside retinal tissue that translates into differential contrast sensitivity.
claims.evidence: This is a central conclusion based on the combination of scattering measurements, simulations, and behavioral data.

claims.claim: The forward scattering characteristic of inverted nuclei mainly suppresses light scattering by nuclear substructure towards large angles, thus preventing image veil and contrast reduction.
claims.source: Specifically, we find that the forward scattering characteristic of inverted nuclei (Kreysing et al., 2010; Solovei et al., 2009) mainly suppresses light scattering by nuclear substructure towards large angles, thus preventing image veil and contrast reduction resulting from it.
claims.evidence: This is based on FACS measurements (Figure 1F, G), simulations (Figure 2D2, E), and MTF measurements (Figure 3).

claims.claim: Chromatin distribution is known to have the potential to modulate the mechanical properties of the nucleus.
claims.source: As an example, chromatin distribution is known to have the potential to modulate the mechanical properties of the nucleus (Kirby and Lammerding, 2018; Miroshnikova et al., 2017; Stephens et al., 2017) and LBR downregulation might even be required for shape changes enabling efficient packing of nuclei (Stephens et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Kirby and Lammerding, 2018; Miroshnikova et al., 2017; Stephens et al., 2017; Stephens et al., 2019.

claims.claim: LBR downregulation might be required for shape changes enabling efficient packing of nuclei.
claims.source: As an example, chromatin distribution is known to have the potential to modulate the mechanical properties of the nucleus (Kirby and Lammerding, 2018; Miroshnikova et al., 2017; Stephens et al., 2017) and LBR downregulation might even be required for shape changes enabling efficient packing of nuclei (Stephens et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by a citation to Stephens et al., 2019.

claims.claim: The increase in intensity of a point stimulus at the photoreceptor level could aid a thresholded or otherwise non-linear readout of rod cells.
claims.source: Lastly, although the size of the PSF is beyond the acuity limit of nocturnal vision, the increase in intensity of a point stimulus at the photoreceptor level could aid a thresholded or otherwise non-linear readout of rod cells, a long-standing hypothesis in the field of visual neuroscience (Barlow, 1956; Field and Rieke, 2002; Nelson, 2017) which was substantiated by the use of quantum-based single-photon sources (Tinsley et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citations to Barlow, 1956; Field and Rieke, 2002; Nelson, 2017; Tinsley et al., 2016.

claims.claim: The larger spacing of photoreceptor segments in the diurnal retina significantly reduces ONL thickness.
claims.source: Firstly, the larger spacing of photoreceptor segments in the diurnal retina significantly reduces ONL thickness (Solovei et al., 2009; Sterling and Laughlin, 2015; Werner and Chalupa, 2004; Williams and Moody, 2004) and thereby the risk of scattering induced veil and loss of image contrast.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Solovei et al., 2009; Sterling and Laughlin, 2015; Werner and Chalupa, 2004; Williams and Moody, 2004.

claims.claim: Shot-noise that accounts for image granularity becomes less of a problem with increasing light levels.
claims.source: Furthermore, as is well known from photography, shot-noise that accounts for image granularity (Barlow, 1956; de Vries, 1943; Rose, 1948) becomes less of a problem with increasing light levels.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Barlow, 1956; de Vries, 1943; Rose, 1948.

claims.claim: Million-fold higher light intensities during the day imply a higher safety margin from the noise floor.
claims.source: Million-fold higher light intensities during the day imply a higher safety margin from this noise floor (Warrant, 1999), (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F,G), as required for neural mechanisms of contrast enhancement to function (Artal et al., 2004; Flevaris and Murray, 2015; Hess et al., 1998; Shevell et al., 1992).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Warrant, 1999; Artal et al., 2004; Flevaris and Murray, 2015; Hess et al., 1998; Shevell et al., 1992.

claims.claim: Although nuclear inversion improves retinal contrast transmission via reduced image veil, resolution remains largely unaffected.
claims.source: Last, but not least, our measurements show that, although nuclear inversion improves retinal contrast transmission via reduced image veil, resolution, the limiting factor for high acuity diurnal vision, remains largely unaffected.
claims.evidence: This is based on PSF measurements showing no change in resolution (Figure 3E2).

claims.claim: Reduced efficiency of canonical DNA repair mechanisms in highly condensed chromocenters could mean a significant disadvantage in the diurnal retina.
claims.source: Besides a reduced need for inverted photoceptor nuclei in diurnal mammals, reduced efficiency of canonical DNA repair mechanisms (Frohns et al., 2014) in highly condensed chromocenters, could mean a significant disadvantage in the diurnal retina and susceptibility to stress and degeneration (Boudard et al., 2011; Dyer, 2016), could also mean a significantly higher cost for inverted nuclei in diurnal species, as their retinae are intrinsically strongly exposed to high-energy, ultra-violet photons.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citations to Frohns et al., 2014; Boudard et al., 2011; Dyer, 2016.

claims.claim: Rod nuclear inversion is necessary and sufficient to explain optically enhanced contrast sensitivity in mice.
claims.source: In conclusion, we showed that rod nuclear inversion is necessary and sufficient to explain optically enhanced contrast sensitivity in mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, based on the combination of all experimental results including MTF measurements, behavioral tests, and rescue experiments.

claims.claim: Downregulation of the lamina tether LBR enables fusion of mobilized chromocenters and thereby an architectural inversion of mouse rod nuclei.
claims.source: Downregulation of the lamina tether LBR (yellow) enables fusion of mobilized chromocenters and thereby an architectural inversion of mouse rod nuclei.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the figure legend for Figure 1B1 and supported by the TG-LBR experiments.

claims.claim: The inner retina alone transmits approximately 50% more image detail than the full retina.
claims.source: Quantification of image transmission shows that the inner retina alone (Rd1/Cpfl1-KO, N = 5) transmits approximately 50% more image detail than the full retina (N = 11), suggesting significant image degradation in the thick outer nuclear layer.
claims.evidence: This is based on experimental measurements shown in Figure 1B3.

claims.claim: Volume-specific light scattering is significantly reduced in the retinal cell nuclei.
claims.source: Volume-specific light scattering is significantly reduced in the retinal cell nuclei.
claims.evidence: This is based on FACS measurements shown in Figure 1C inset.

claims.claim: Quantification of reduced scattering with chromocenter number is sufficiently explained by a wave optical model of light scattering.
claims.source: Quantification of reduced scattering with chromocenter number is sufficiently explained by a wave optical model of light scattering n = 38 nuclei.
claims.evidence: This is based on comparison of experimental data with Mie scattering calculations shown in Figure 1H.

claims.claim: In inverted rod nuclei, the chromatin of the central chromocenter and the surrounding shell of LINE-rich heterochromatin is packed so densely that free molecules of GFP do not penetrate into these nuclear regions.
claims.source: In inverted rod nuclei, the chromatin of the central chromocenter (arrows) and the surrounding shell of LINE-rich heterochromatin (arrowheads) is packed so densely that free molecules of GFP do not penetrate into these nuclear regions.
claims.evidence: This is based on microscopy observations shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: In conventional nuclei, the entire nucleoplasm, regardless to chromatin nature, is penetrable for GFP with chromocenters showing slightly less permeability.
claims.source: In conventional nuclei, exemplified by ganglion and bipolar cells, the entire nucleoplasm, regardless to chromatin nature, is penetrable for GFP with chromocenters showing slightly less permeability (arrows).

results.result: Rod photoreceptors in nocturnal mammals display inverted nuclear architecture where heterochromatin is centrally located and euchromatin is at the periphery, a feature exclusive to nocturnal mammals that has been proposed as an evolutionary adaptation to low-light conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C11, C13, C14 are well-established findings from prior work (supported by multiple citations to Błaszczak et al., 2014; Kreysing et al., 2010; Solovei et al., 2009, 2013) and confirmed by microscopy data in Figure 1B1. The evolutionary hypothesis (C2, C15) is appropriately attributed to prior work. This represents established background knowledge for the study.

results.result: The outer nuclear layer (ONL) containing rod nuclei significantly impacts light propagation in the mouse retina, as demonstrated by 49-50% greater image detail transmission when photoreceptors and their nuclei are absent (Rd1/Cpfl1-KO mice).
results.evaluation: Claims C20, C23, C78 are supported by direct experimental comparison between WT and Rd1/Cpfl1-KO retinae (Figure 1B3). The measurements are clear and the conclusion that rod nuclei impact light transmission is well-justified. Sample sizes are reported (N=5 for KO, N=11 for WT).

results.result: Retinal cells, predominantly rod photoreceptors, are optically specialized and scatter substantially less light than brain neurons and neuroblastoma cells, with significantly reduced volume-specific light scattering.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C26, C79 are supported by FACS measurements (Figure 1C) comparing different cell types. The normalization by volume (forward scattering as proxy for size) is appropriate. The conclusion of optical specialization is reasonable given the comparative data, though the mechanism (C27) remains speculative.

results.result: During retinal development, sideward light scattering decreases significantly in adult nuclei compared to P25 stage, with nuclei containing fewer chromocenters scattering less light, a trend reproduced by wave-optical Mie scattering models.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C30, C80 are supported by FACS measurements (Figure 1F, G) and theoretical Mie calculations (Figure 1H). The correlation between chromocenter number and scattering is demonstrated experimentally (n=38 nuclei) and the theoretical model provides mechanistic support. The agreement between experiment and theory strengthens the conclusion.

results.result: In TG-LBR mice where LBR overexpression prevents chromocenter fusion, >70% of rod nuclei are arrested with multiple chromocenters, resulting in significantly increased light scattering comparable to P14 WT pups, establishing a causal relationship between chromocenter fusion and reduced scattering.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C35, C77, C84-C87 are supported by microscopy (Figures 2A, B, Figure 1—figure supplement 2) and FACS measurements (Figure 2C). The TG-LBR model is well-characterized (Solovei et al., 2013) and the arrest efficiency (>70%) is quantified (Figure 2—figure supplement 2). The causal conclusion (C35) is justified by the genetic intervention showing that preventing fusion increases scattering.

results.result: Computational simulations and optical modeling demonstrate that chromocenter fusion reduces large-angle scattering (>30°) through decreased volume-specific scattering and reduced geometric scattering cross-section, thereby reducing scattering-induced veil and preventing contrast losses.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C38, C88, C104 are supported by computational simulations (Figure 2D2, E), theoretical calculations (Figure 2F, G), and optical reconstitution experiments with silica beads (Figure 2H). The simulations use anatomically faithful nuclear positions (~1750 nuclei) and the physical explanation via Mie scattering theory is sound. The bead experiment provides independent validation.

results.result: Wildtype retinae improve contrast transmission throughout terminal development, with adult retinae showing consistently elevated MTFs compared to P14 developmental stages, representing a 2-fold improvement in optical quality (Strehl ratio) and ~49% better contrast transfer at visually relevant spatial frequencies.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C39, C40, C42, C90 are supported by extensive MTF measurements (>1300 images, N=19 adult, N=18 P14 animals, Figure 3A, C). The Strehl ratio calculations are appropriate and the developmental improvement is clearly demonstrated. The comparison to lens development (Tkatchenko et al., 2010) provides context.

results.result: Developmental improvements in retinal optical quality do not occur in TG-LBR mice where nuclear inversion is arrested, with Strehl ratios 1.91±0.14 fold lower than WT adults (p=3.4×10⁻⁸), demonstrating that nuclear inversion causes the enhancement in retinal optical quality.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C43, C45, C91 are supported by MTF measurements in TG-LBR mice (N=18 animals, Figure 3B, D). The genetic intervention provides strong evidence for causality. Statistical significance is reported and sample sizes are adequate. The comparison between WT adult, WT P14, and TG-LBR adult is comprehensive.

results.result: The monotonic decay of retina-transmitted contrast indicates that contrast loss is caused by scattering-induced veil rather than frequency cut-off, with contrast lost due to generation of image veil from side scattering that overcasts attenuated signals.
results.evaluation: Claims C41, C49 are supported by the shape of MTF curves (Figures 3A, B, Figure 3—figure supplement 2A-D) and the combination of MTF, PSF, and scattering measurements. The interpretation that monotonic decay indicates veil rather than cut-off is standard in optical analysis and is consistent with the scattering data.

results.result: Nuclear inversion improves retinal contrast transmission with ~2-fold higher peak PSF intensity in WT vs TG-LBR retinae, but does not affect resolution (FWHM: 4.32±2.38 μm WT vs 3.75±2.01 μm TG-LBR), indicating enhancement of contrast but not acuity.
results.evaluation: Claims C18, C46-C48, C74, C92 are supported by PSF measurements (N=119 WT, N=121 TG-LBR, 6 animals total, Figure 3E1, E2). The lack of resolution difference is important for establishing the specific mechanism. The measurements independently corroborate the MTF findings and clarify that the benefit is contrast, not resolution.

results.result: Despite differential image signal quality, overall photon transmission through rhodopsin-bleached retinae is nearly identical between WT (74±8%) and TG-LBR (72±5%) mice, indicating that photon arrival at photoreceptor outer segments remains unchanged.
results.evaluation: Claims C50, C93 are based on diffuse transmission measurements (Figure 3E3), but sample size is very small (n=2 animals each). While the measurements support the conclusion that total photon transmission is unchanged, the limited replication raises concerns about statistical power. Additional replicates would strengthen this important control showing that the effect is on contrast, not photon budget.

results.result: Under scotopic conditions (20 and 2 mLux), WT mice show 18-27% higher overall contrast sensitivity than TG-LBR mice (measured by AULC), with significant differences appearing above 0.15 cycles/degree, while no differences are observed at photopic conditions (70 Lux).
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C52-C57, C95-C97 are supported by optomotor response measurements (N=10-11 animals per group, Figure 4B, C, D). Controls with Rho-/- mice confirm rod pathway dependence (C54). Statistical tests are appropriate (t-tests, p-values reported). Note: There is a discrepancy between text (18%, 27%) and figure legend (22%, 29%) for C55/C96, but both support the overall conclusion of improved sensitivity.

results.result: At spatial frequencies near visual acuity (0.26-0.30 cycles/degree), WT mice show up to 10-fold greater positive response rates at intermediate contrasts and 6-fold reduced risk of missing stimuli at high contrasts compared to TG-LBR mice, representing improved motion detection capabilities.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C58, C59, C98, C99 are supported by detailed optomotor response measurements at specific spatial frequencies and contrasts (Figure 4E). The 10-fold difference at intermediate contrasts (29% vs 3% correct response) and 6-fold difference in miss rates (11% vs 59%) are dramatic and statistically significant (p<0.0001, Chi-square test). Sample sizes are adequate (N=210, N=60, N=90, N=90 trials).

results.result: The 18-27% difference in behavioral contrast sensitivity correlates with a 26% higher Strehl ratio in WT retinae at relevant frequencies (0-0.36 cycles/degree), suggesting that at low light levels, contrast sensitivity may be directly limited by retinal contrast transmission.
results.evaluation: Claims C60, C61 are supported by comparison of behavioral data (Figure 4C) with MTF-derived Strehl ratios. The correlation between optical measurements and behavioral outcomes is strong and the interpretation is reasonable. However, correlation does not prove causation, which is addressed by the rescue experiment (C62-C63).

results.result: When displayed contrasts are adjusted to pre-compensate for differential retinal contrast loss, visual competence of TG-LBR mice is rescued to near-identical levels as WT mice, demonstrating that improved retinal contrast transmission is sufficient to explain increased contrast sensitivity.
results.evaluation: Claims C62, C63, C100, C101 are supported by rescue experiments (Figure 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C). This is a critical experiment that establishes sufficiency and rules out non-specific effects of LBR overexpression. The logic is sound: if the behavioral deficit can be rescued by optical compensation, then the deficit is optical in nature. This is analogous to molecular rescue experiments.

results.result: Rod nuclear inversion is necessary and sufficient to explain optically enhanced contrast sensitivity in mice, with improved image quality transmitted by the retina enabling greater contrast sensitivity exclusively at nocturnal conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C76, C106 represent the main conclusion, supported by the combination of: (1) developmental correlation (C39-C42), (2) genetic necessity (TG-LBR arrests inversion and prevents optical improvement, C43-C45), (3) behavioral consequences specific to scotopic conditions (C52-C59), and (4) sufficiency demonstrated by rescue (C62-C63). The evidence is comprehensive and the logic is sound.

results.result: The direction of light scattering inside retinal tissue translates into differential contrast sensitivity, with inverted nuclei suppressing large-angle scattering by nuclear substructure, leading to ~2-fold improvement in retinal contrast transmission.
results.evaluation: Claims C66, C67, C104, C105 synthesize the mechanistic findings from scattering measurements (Figure 1F, G), simulations (Figure 2D2, E), and MTF measurements (Figure 3D). The conclusion that directional scattering matters is well-supported by the data showing that large-angle scattering is specifically reduced and this correlates with improved contrast transmission.

results.result: Eye size (anterior-posterior and naso-temporal/superior-inferior axes) and lens diameter are comparable between WT and TG-LBR adult mice, indicating no gross anatomical differences.
results.evaluation: Claims C102, C103 are supported by anatomical measurements (N=9 eyes each for eye size, N=19 lenses each, Figure 4—figure supplement 2A, B). This is an important control to rule out confounding anatomical differences. Sample sizes are adequate for detecting major differences.

results.result: The unique optical property of rod cells could stem from unusually dense packing of heterochromatin in the nuclear center, which is so dense that free GFP molecules do not penetrate these regions in inverted nuclei.
results.evaluation: Claims C27, C81, C82 are based on GFP exclusion data (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B). While the observation is clear, the causal link to optical properties (C27) is speculative. The dense packing could contribute to optical specialization, but this is not directly tested. The claim is appropriately hedged with 'could stem from' but remains a hypothesis.

results.result: Nuclear inversion may serve additional functions beyond improved contrast sensitivity, including modulation of nuclear mechanical properties, efficient nuclear packing, or enhanced thresholded readout of rod cells, though these remain speculative.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C70, C75 are appropriately presented as speculation in the Discussion. They are supported by citations to relevant literature but are not tested in this study. These represent reasonable hypotheses for future work but do not constitute findings of the current manuscript.

results.result: Background knowledge about retinal anatomy, nocturnal vision, and light scattering properties is established through citations to prior work.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C10, C12, C16-C17, C21-C22, C64-C65, C71-C73 represent established knowledge from the literature, appropriately cited. These provide necessary context for the study but are not novel findings. The citations appear appropriate and the knowledge claims are standard in the field.

results.result: During the first 4-6 weeks of postnatal development, conventional nuclear architecture of rod progenitors is gradually rearranged into inverted architecture of mature rods, with retinal layer structure preserved in TG-LBR mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C83, C89 are supported by microscopy observations (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 2). These are descriptive findings that establish the developmental timeline and confirm that TG-LBR mice maintain normal retinal stratification despite arrested nuclear inversion.

results.result: Micro-projection experiments suggest that nuclear inversion results in cat images becoming visible at greater distances (0.70 vs 0.45 meters) for WT compared to TG-LBR mice, indicating better predator detection potential.
results.evaluation: Claims C51, C94 are based on micro-projection experiments (Figure 3G) but the threshold is described as 'arbitrary' and the ecological relevance is unclear. While the demonstration is illustrative, it lacks the rigor of the quantitative MTF and behavioral measurements. This is more of an illustrative example than a rigorous result.
